concept.technique_name: distance and gradient between two points

examples.problem_statement: In Figure 21.13(b), find length AB and gradient of AB given points A(2,3) and B(8,7).

solution.description: Read the two given points off the problem and label them: A(2, 3) is the first point and B(8, 7) the second. Fixing the order now keeps every later difference consistent.
Subtract the x-coordinate of A from the x-coordinate of B, 8 minus 2, to get a horizontal run of 6 units. This is one leg of the right triangle sitting under AB.
Subtract the y-coordinate of A from the y-coordinate of B, 7 minus 3, to get a vertical rise of 4 units, the second leg of that right triangle.

solution.operation: Calculate length AB using distance formula
solution.description: With legs of 6 and 4 known, apply Pythagoras: square each, add them to get 52, and take the square root, so the straight-line length AB is about 7.211 units.
The gradient is rise over run, so divide the vertical difference 4 by the horizontal difference 6 and cancel to two-thirds. Using the same point order as in steps 2 and 3 keeps the sign right.

common_mistakes: Dividing the horizontal difference by the vertical one, giving a gradient of 6/4 instead of 4/6.
Subtracting the coordinates in opposite orders for x and y (8 minus 2 but 3 minus 7), which flips the sign of the gradient.
Adding 6 and 4 to get 10 instead of squaring them first, which loses the square root of 52.

concept.technique_name: trigonometric ratios in degrees and minutes

examples.problem_statement: In triangle EFG in Figure 21.16, calculate angle G

solution.operation: Identify the type of triangle and relevant sides
solution.result: \text{Right triangle with hypotenuse } = 8.71, \text{ opposite to } \angle G = 2.30
solution.description: Read the figure for triangle EFG: the side of length 2.30 lies opposite angle G and 8.71 is the hypotenuse. Naming the sides relative to angle G is what decides the ratio to use.
Because the known pair is the opposite side and the hypotenuse, sine is the ratio that links them to angle G.

solution.operation: Substitute the known values into the sine formula
solution.description: Substitute the two measured lengths into that ratio, opposite side 2.30 on top and hypotenuse 8.71 underneath.
Divide 2.30 by 8.71 to get sin G as a decimal, 0.26406429. Carry the extra decimal places forward instead of rounding here, so the angle stays accurate.
The sine of the angle is known but the angle is not, so apply the inverse sine to 0.26406429 to undo the sine.
Evaluate that inverse sine with the calculator in degree mode: angle G is 15.31136 degrees, which rounds to 15.31 degrees.

solution.operation: Convert decimal degrees to degrees and minutes
solution.description: To restate the answer in degrees and minutes, multiply only the decimal part, 0.31, by 60. That gives 18.6 minutes, which rounds to 19, so angle G is 15 degrees 19 minutes.

examples.problem_statement: Evaluate the following expression, correct to 3 significant figures: (4.2 tan 49°26′ − 3.7 sin 66°1′) / (7.1 cos 29°34′)

solution.description: Rewrite 49 degrees 26 minutes as a decimal angle by dividing 26 by 60 and adding it to 49, then take the tangent, giving 1.1681.
Convert the other two angles the same way and evaluate them: sin 66 degrees 1 minute is 0.9137 and cos 29 degrees 34 minutes is 0.8698.
Substitute the three decimal values back into the expression and carry out the multiplications: 4.2 times 1.1681, 3.7 times 0.9137, and 7.1 times 0.8698.
Finish the numerator by subtracting 3.3807 from 4.9060 to get 1.5253, and the denominator by evaluating 7.1 times 0.8698 as 6.1756.
Divide 1.5253 by 6.1756 to get 0.2470, which to 3 significant figures is 0.247.

examples.problem_statement: In the triangle ABC shown in Figure 21.19, find the lengths AC and AB

solution.description: List what the figure gives for right triangle ABC: side BC is 6.2 mm and angle B is 42 degrees. One side plus one acute angle is enough to find everything else.
AC lies opposite angle B and BC lies adjacent to it, so tangent is the ratio connecting them: tan 42 degrees equals AC over 6.2.
Multiply both sides by 6.2 to release AC. With tan 42 degrees equal to 0.9004, AC comes to 5.58248 mm.
For AB, the known side BC is adjacent to angle B and AB is the hypotenuse, so switch to cosine: cos 42 degrees equals 6.2 over AB.
AB sits in the denominator, so rearrange to AB equals 6.2 divided by cos 42 degrees. Dividing 6.2 by 0.7431 gives 8.343 mm.
Check AB a second way, independent of the cosine: Pythagoras on the two legs just found, 5.58248 and 6.2, also gives 8.343 mm.
Round both results to the 2 decimal places the question asks for, giving AC as 5.58 mm and AB as 8.34 mm.

examples.answer: AC = 5.58 mm, AB = 8.34 mm (rounded to 2 decimal places)

examples.problem_statement: Sketch a right-angled triangle ABC such that B = 90°, AB = 5 cm and BC = 12 cm. Determine the length of AC and hence evaluate sin A, cos C and tan A

solution.description: The right angle is at B, so AC is the hypotenuse. Square the legs 5 and 12, add to get 169, and take the root: AC is 13 cm.
For angle A the opposite side is BC at 12 cm and the hypotenuse is AC at 13 cm, so sin A is 12 over 13, which is 0.9231.
For angle C the adjacent side is that same BC of 12 cm over the same hypotenuse of 13 cm, so cos C is also 0.9231, as expected since A and C are complementary.
For tan A use only the two sides about the right angle: opposite BC at 12 cm over adjacent AB at 5 cm, giving 2.400.

examples.problem_statement: In triangle PQR shown in Figure 21.21, find the lengths of PQ and PR

solution.description: In triangle PQR, PQ is opposite the 38 degree angle and QR of 7.5 cm is adjacent to it, so tangent links them: tan 38 degrees equals PQ over 7.5.
Multiply both sides by 7.5 to isolate PQ. With tan 38 degrees equal to 0.7813, PQ is 5.860 cm.

For each triangle, we need to know: 1) Which angle is the right angle, and 2) The positions of the given sides relative to the angles. Without this information, multiple configurations are possible.

examples.problem_statement: The angle of depression of a ship viewed at a particular instant from the top of a 75 m vertical cliff is 30°. Find the distance of the ship from the base of the cliff at this instant. The ship is sailing away from the cliff at constant speed and 1 minute later its angle of depression from the top of the cliff is 20°. Determine the speed of the ship in km/h

solution.description: Sketch the situation first: a vertical cliff 75 m high with the observer at the top, and the ship at two positions as the angle of depression falls from 30 degrees to 20 degrees over one minute.

The angle of depression at the top equals the angle at the ship between the horizontal and the line of sight, so in that right triangle the 75 m cliff is opposite and the distance from the base is adjacent: tan 30 degrees equals 75 over d1.
Rearrange to make d1 the subject and divide 75 by tan 30 degrees, which gives 129.90 m as the ship's first distance from the base of the cliff.
Set up the same relationship for the later sighting, when the angle has dropped to 20 degrees because the ship has moved further out: tan 20 degrees equals 75 over d2.
Divide 75 by tan 20 degrees, about 0.3640, to get the second distance, 206.04 m from the base of the cliff.
Subtract the first distance from the second: the ship covered 76.14 m, and it covered it in the one minute between the two sightings.
Turn 76.14 metres per minute into kilometres per hour by multiplying by the 60 minutes in an hour and dividing by the 1000 metres in a kilometre, which gives 4.568.
Round that speed to the 3 significant figures the question expects, so the ship is sailing at 4.57 km/h.

key_reminders: {'point': 'Remember: Angle of depression equals alternate interior angle when horizontal line and sight line form parallel lines with transversal.'}
{'point': 'Caution: Always ensure units are consistent — here, meters converted to kilometers and seconds to hours for final answer in km/h.'}
{'point': 'Speed tip: Practice unit conversions like m/s to km/h (multiply by 3.6) for faster calculations.'}

Multiplying 75 by tan 30 degrees instead of dividing, which gives a distance shorter than the cliff is tall.
Reporting 76.14 as the speed in km/h and skipping the conversion from metres per minute.

concept.technique_name: graphs of sine, cosine and tangent

examples.problem_statement: Plot the graphs of y = sin A, y = cos A, and y = tan A for values of A from 0° to 360°.

solution.description: Identify the three trigonometric functions to be plotted and their key characteristics over one full period (0° to 360°).

solution.operation: Create a table of key values
solution.description: Calculate values at critical angles (0°, 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°) to establish key points for plotting.

Plot points: (0°,0), (90°,1), (180°,0), (270°,-1), (360°,0). Connect with a smooth curve showing the wave pattern. The sine function starts at 0, peaks at 90°, crosses at 180°, troughs at 270°, and returns to 0 at 360°.
Plot points: (0°,1), (90°,0), (180°,-1), (270°,0), (360°,1). Connect with a smooth curve. The cosine function starts at 1, crosses at 90°, troughs at 180°, crosses at 270°, and returns to 1 at 360°.

Plot points between asymptotes: (0°,0), (45°,1), (135°,-1), (180°,0), (225°,1), (315°,-1). Draw vertical asymptotes at 90° and 270° where cos A = 0. The curve approaches +∞ at 90° from the left and -∞ from the right, repeating this pattern every 180°.
Label all axes, curves, key points, and asymptotes. Verify that all functions show correct periodicity and behavior: sine and cosine have period 360°, tangent has period 180°.

examples.answer: The graphs should show: y = sin A is a sine wave starting at 0, peaking at 90°, crossing at 180°, troughing at 270°, and returning to 0 at 360°. y = cos A is a cosine wave starting at 1, crossing at 90°, troughing at 180°, crossing at 270°, and returning to 1 at 360°. y = tan A has vertical asymptotes at 90° and 270°, with the curve approaching infinity and negative infinity respectively.

concept.technique_name: inverse cosine: all angles between 0 and 360 degrees

examples.problem_statement: In Figure 22.10, angle θ = cos⁻¹(0.2348) = 76.42°. Measured from 0°, the two angles whose cosine is −0.2348 are α = 180° − 76.42°, i.e. 103.58° and α = 180° + 76.42°, i.e. 256.42°

solution.description: Start from the reference angle supplied: the acute angle whose cosine is positive 0.2348 is 76.42 degrees. Both required solutions will be measured from this angle.

Recall the symmetry of the cosine function, which takes the same value at an angle and at its reflection about the horizontal axis. That symmetry lets one reference angle generate every solution within a full turn.
The equation actually asks for cosine equal to negative 0.2348. Cosine is negative in the second and third quadrants, so both answers lie between 90 and 270 degrees.
Place the reference angle in the second quadrant by subtracting it from 180 degrees: 180 minus 76.42 gives the first solution, 103.58 degrees.
Place the same reference angle in the third quadrant by adding it to 180 degrees: 180 plus 76.42 gives the second solution, 256.42 degrees.
Confirm both by evaluating their cosines: 103.58 degrees and 256.42 degrees each give about negative 0.2348, and both lie inside the 0 to 360 degree range.

key_reminders: {'point': 'Now try the following Practice Exercise; (answers on page 349); In problems 4 to 6, solve the given equations in the range 0° to 360°, giving the answers in degrees and minutes.'}
common_mistakes: Using 360 minus 76.42, which lands in the fourth quadrant where cosine is positive, instead of the second and third quadrant angles a negative cosine requires.
Measuring the reference angle from 90 degrees rather than 180 degrees when placing it in a quadrant.
Stopping at one answer, when a cosine equation has two solutions between 0 and 360 degrees.
